identity.title: Ice-pack test (ptosis improves >=2 mm after 2 min ice)

technique.how: Measure the palpebral fissure of the ptotic eye, then hold an ice pack (in a glove or towel) firmly over the closed lid for 2 minutes and immediately re-measure. Positive if the fissure widens by 2 mm or more.
technique.prerequisites: Measurable ptosis; ruler; patient able to keep eye closed for 2 minutes.
technique.contraindications: Cold urticaria or facial cold injury; minimal or complete ptosis limits interpretation.

interpretation.positive_finding: Improvement of >=2 mm strongly supports myasthenic ptosis (RCE summary LR+ 24; in the index study 16/20 MG vs 0/20 non-MG ptosis).
interpretation.negative_finding: No improvement lowers the probability (summary LR- 0.16) but does not exclude MG, especially with complete ptosis where 3 of 4 patients tested negative.
interpretation.pitfalls: Studies are small, case-control, and from neuro-ophthalmology clinics with high MG prevalence, so LRs may be inflated. Ice must be applied long enough and measurement done immediately.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: treat as probable MG and send AChR antibodies/EMG; negative: still test if fatigable weakness or bulbar symptoms are present.

estimates.target_condition: Myasthenia gravis in patients with ptosis
estimates.population: Patients with ptosis in included studies (mostly neuro-ophthalmology clinic case series, high MG prevalence)
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical/serologic/electrophysiologic diagnosis of MG per included studies
estimates.quote: The ice test is useful when the response is abnormal (summary positive LR, 24.0; 95% CI, 8.5-67.0) and diminishes the likelihood of myasthenia gravis when the response is normal (summary negative LR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.09-0.27)

estimates.population: 20 MG patients with ptosis and 20 control patients with nonmyasthenic ptosis, multicenter neuro-ophthalmology services (case-control)
estimates.reference_standard: Established diagnosis of MG vs other cause of ptosis
estimates.quote: A positive ice test result was noted in 16 of the 20 (80%) patients with MG and in none of the 20 patients without MG (P < 0.001)

sources.citation: Scherer K, Bedlack RS, Simel DL. Does this patient have myasthenia gravis? JAMA 2005;293:1906-1914.
Golnik KC, Pena R, Lee AG, Eggenberger ER. An ice test for the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. Ophthalmology 1999;106:1282-1286.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not useful without ptosis; do not use a negative test to dismiss MG in a patient with bulbar or respiratory symptoms.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Dysphagia, dyspnea or a falling single-breath count suggests impending myasthenic crisis; monitor respiratory function and escalate regardless of ice test result.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Measurement to 1 mm with a ruler; 2 mm threshold is arbitrary and no reproducibility data were found.

extraction_notes: RCE summary LRs from abstract (table not accessible). Golnik 1999 sens/spec from abstract counts; prevalence 0.5 reflects case-control design, not a clinical prevalence. Specificity 1.0 makes LR+ undefined so LRs not computed for that entry.
